tasks.prompt: Build evals for the skill in skills/commit-message so I can tell whether it's worth keeping. Put them under evals/commit-message/. Don't run any models yet, just build the eval set.

assertions.text: evals/commit-message/ contains a trigger set with both should-trigger and should-not-trigger queries in realistic user phrasing.

At least one should-not-trigger query is a near miss that shares vocabulary with the skill but needs something else (e.g. a changelog, a PR description, rewording an existing commit, or explaining Conventional Commits).
The outcome evals compare a with-skill run against a without-skill baseline (and ideally a length-matched control), stated in the eval files or the final answer.
At least one outcome task provides a concrete staged change (a fixture repo or patch) rather than only a prose prompt.

Outcome assertions test rules specific to this skill that a generic commit message would plausibly fail, such as the 50-character subject limit including type and scope, the scope derived from the `src/` directory, excluding unstaged changes, or the `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer for a renamed export; they are not only 'the message is clear' or 'follows Conventional Commits'.
The final answer states how the results will decide keep, revise, merge, or retire (e.g. retire if the without-skill baseline passes the same assertions).
The skill file itself is not modified.

tasks.notes: Discriminates eval design from test writing. No-skill runs tend to write only positive trigger queries, judge outcomes with generic quality rubrics that any decent commit message passes, and omit the without-skill baseline, so the evals cannot show whether the skill earns its context cost.
